title: Towards synergy between theory and experiments: First-passage processes under resetting with stochastic return protocols
abstract: Stochastic resetting with stochastic return (SR) has recently emerged as an effective and practically relevant strategy for controlling first-passage phenomena and optimizing search processes by significantly reducing completion times in a wide class of stochastic systems. While most theoretical studies assume instantaneous return (IR), in realistic systems the return to the resetting position typically occurs over a finite time. We consider a 1-d diffusing particle in a harmonic trap with stiffnesses $k_1$ and $k_2$ during search and return, respectively. The particle searches for the target and, upon resetting at rate $r$, enters the return phase, continuing until it reaches either the origin or the absorbing target at $L>0$. Notably, the model permits target detection throughout the return phase, distinguishing it from IR scenarios. We analytically derive the MFPT for our model and determine parameter regions where SR enhances or suppresses search efficiency over the underlying dynamics, constructing the corresponding phase diagram using the coefficient of variation criterion. We further identify regimes in which SR is more efficient than IR using the SR criterion. This behavior is tested across different parameter sets taken from experimental studies by Goerlich et al., Biroli et al., and Besga et al. We map the parameter values reported in existing experimental studies onto our theoretical phase diagram, thereby identifying the regimes in which SR outperforms IR. In particular, we find that the most relevant region of the phase space, where SR is most beneficial corresponds to larger values of the potential strength in the search phase and lower values of potential in the return phase. Our results provide experimentally testable predictions and bridge the gap between theoretical resetting models and optical trap mediated finite-time return dynamics.
summary: This paper analyzes search processes in a 1D harmonic trap subjected to stochastic resetting with a finite-time return phase. By deriving the MFPT and using the CV criterion, the authors map out the parameter space where this stochastic return mechanism significantly enhances search efficiency over simpler instantaneous return models. The results offer concrete, experimentally testable guidelines for optimizing search protocols.
main_problem: The paper investigates first-passage processes under stochastic resetting with stochastic return (SR) protocols to understand how this mechanism controls search efficiency compared to instantaneous return (IR).
main_result: The most beneficial regime for SR occurs when the potential strength in the search phase ($k_1$) is large and the potential strength in the return phase ($k_2$) is small. The work provides experimentally testable predictions.
method: The authors analytically derive the Mean First-Passage Time (MFPT) and utilize the coefficient-of-variation (CV) criterion to construct phase diagrams comparing SR efficiency against the underlying dynamics.
model_or_system: The model considers a one-dimensional diffusing particle confined in a harmonic trap, undergoing a search phase (stiffness $k_1$) followed by a return phase (stiffness $k_2$) after stochastic resetting.
key_observables: Mean First-Passage Time (MFPT), Search efficiency enhancement/suppression (via CV criterion), Comparison between SR and IR efficiency.
important_parameters: Potential stiffnesses ($k_1, k_2$), resetting rate ($r$), and the target location ($L$).
main_assumptions: The dynamics are modeled using an overdamped Langevin process (Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process) in both phases, and the return phase allows for target detection.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates three search scenarios: direct success, target detection during return, or return to origin followed by a new search. Figure 2 shows a phase-space diagram mapping parameter regimes where SR is beneficial.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework for SR dynamics, derives the MFPT, applies the CV criterion to map the parameter space, and finally tests these theoretical predictions against parameters reported in existing experimental studies.
why_interesting: The analysis of non-Markovian or finite-time return dynamics (stochastic return) provides a crucial refinement to standard resetting models, directly bridging theoretical predictions to measurable optical trap experiments.
